prize_parts.citation: for developing empirical methods to estimate demand, market power and industry dynamics in differentiated-product markets

statement.case_for: The Berry inversion, BLP and Pakes's related estimation work gave economists a general way to recover demand, markups and welfare effects from market data with endogenous prices. Thirty years of use have confirmed the approach. It is a standard tool in merger review and competition policy, and it is used in trade, health, environmental and public economics. The contribution combines theory, identification and computation, and it yields replicable empirical results. Attribution is the cleanest available for a three-name prize: Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes are the BLP core, and Pakes's dynamic-industry strand fits under the same citation without adding names. After reading colleagues' openings I still rate it highly on breadth of impact across fields and on maturity. I do not rank it highly because of any support count. Nothing in the other openings changes my view of its scientific standing.
statement.case_against: This is a methodological contribution, and some colleagues may prefer a substantive discovery about economic phenomena. The three-name cap leaves out Bresnahan and Reiss, who have real claims on the empirical-IO revolution, as well as Benkard and Levin on the dynamic side. The credited set on the ballot is broader than any three-person prize. Whether to split credit between the demand-side (BLP) and dynamic-game (Pakes) strands is a judgement call. Results also depend on functional form, instruments and computational implementation. The strongest reservation is that a prize built on the BLP trio could look arbitrary to those who see the structural-IO programme as a larger collective achievement.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B022 first, regards BLP as the cleanest core, and asks whether Bresnahan's earlier demand-system and market-power work should displace Levinsohn.
responses.response: I agree on the BLP core and on Pakes's separate standing in dynamic games. I would keep Levinsohn. The discovery described here is estimating demand with endogenous prices and unobserved heterogeneity, and that is the Berry-Levinsohn-Pakes contribution. Bresnahan's work on market power and demand systems preceded it and is real, but it is a different strand. The cap means that credit is cut, and I would say so openly in the citation rather than pretend the trio exhausts the field. Friberg and I both rank this first, so the committee should treat our agreement with caution, given our overlapping interest in applied microeconomics.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson ranks B037 first on its combination of new data, transparent quasi-experimental designs and an explanatory framework, but notes that the three-person limit forces a choice between Dorn and Katz and that Katz's work partly overlaps prior laureates.
responses.response: I take the credibility-of-design argument seriously, and it moved B037 up in my thinking compared with my opening rank of seventh. My remaining concern is the one Hjalmarsson names. The skill-premium and task strand and the China-shock strand are separable contributions, so a three-name prize either combines them with an awkward Katz-versus-Dorn choice or narrows to the trade-shock work. I would be more comfortable with B037 if the committee settled on a single coherent discovery. As it stands, B022 has the cleaner attribution. I keep B037 as an alternative rather than my preferred option.

responses.point: Teorell ranks B025 (Kiyotaki and Moore) second, with clean attribution to the two originators and strong validation by the 2008 crisis. He also ranks B045 first and B008 third.
responses.response: I agree that the Kiyotaki-Moore attribution is cleaner than almost any other on the list, and I ranked B025 second in my opening. Teorell himself notes that the original model is stylised and that the empirical identification was mostly done by others, and Strömberg raises the 2022 overlap. Those points make me slightly more cautious. The relevance of collateral amplification was confirmed by events, but not through direct tests of the mechanism. B022's methods have been checked repeatedly in applied work. That is why I put B022 ahead, although the two are close and B025 would be a defensible prize.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat structural estimation as a prize-worthy discovery rather than a method, given recent econometrics and mechanism-design awards.
Whether Bresnahan or Reiss should be recognised instead of, or ahead of, one of the BLP trio.
How much weight B037's broad support should carry once the Katz-versus-Dorn attribution is resolved.
My assessments rest on my own knowledge of the literature. I have not independently verified sources.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile with respect to the candidates in B022. My research is in market design and mechanism theory, which is a neighbouring but distinct area. I am also an SSE affiliate alongside committee members Dreber Almenberg, Friberg and Strömberg. That is a colleague connection, not a candidate connection, and I do not treat it as bearing on this choice.
